title: Building a Grid That Dissolves Into Chaos
concept_layer: randomness as the breakdown of order; entropy as a gradient; pseudo-randomness via randf_range
domain_deferred: true randomness vs pseudo-randomness → later randomness maps

capture_leaks.pseudo_vs_true: randf_range uses a deterministic PRNG. Given the same seed, the output is reproducible. True randomness (thermal, quantum) is not available. PRNG internals deferred.
capture_leaks.uniform_distribution: Every offset is drawn from a uniform range. But most natural randomness is Gaussian, Poisson, or power-law. Distribution shapes arrive later.
capture_leaks.independent_samples: Each offset is independent of its neighbors. Natural noise is usually correlated — that's what the next sequence (noise) addresses.
capture_leaks.scalar_entropy: Entropy here is a single float (randomness_amount) at each Z slice. Shannon entropy as information measure requires probability distributions — deferred to QFEP.
capture_leaks.reversibility: The grid dissolves toward high Z, but you can never 'reassemble' it by walking back. The artifact visually reinforces the arrow of time without naming it.

limit: Ten thousand points, a gradient of chaos. It looks like the whole story: order becomes disorder. But this is a mechanical simulation of entropy, not entropy itself. Real entropy is about state counting, information content, the probability-weighted log of microstates. This artifact lets you feel the shape; the statistical mechanics comes later.

grammar_alignment.note: entropy_axiom teaches jitter (per-point random offset) and scatter (distribute many forms in a region) simultaneously — the two operations are easier to teach together because they're the same randf_range call at different scales.

biome_alignment.note: Fungus kingdom unlocks here — the first 'disorganized' life form. Creatures begin appearing (octapod, plasma). The world has started populating itself non-deterministically. The catalyst mode 'chaos' lets the player inject randomness into any form.

stages.title: From wave to noise
stages.thinking: WaveFunctions_Unit_Circle taught that sine is the shadow of a circle — a pure, predictable, memoryless signal. Now its opposite. What if the next value is not derivable from the current one? What if every position is drawn fresh from a hat? This is randomness. The sine is one curve for all time; randomness is a new curve every frame, every draw.
stages.code:
# Sine:
#   y(t) = sin(t)   → deterministic, same t always gives same y
#
# Randomness:
#   y = randf_range(-1, 1)   → each call returns a different value
#   no t dependency, no memory, no predictability
#
# The question becomes:
# if we add randomness to an ordered structure,
# when does order die?

stages.title: Build a perfectly ordered grid
stages.thinking: Start with the opposite of random: a regular 10×10×40 grid of points. Each point sits at a computed position (x·s, y·s, z·s). No randomness yet. This is order as infrastructure. Every point knows exactly where it belongs. The triple nested for-loop is the pattern that scales arrays to 3D volumes.

stages.title: The chaos gradient — entropy grows with Z
stages.thinking: The crucial move. entropy_factor = z / (grid_size_z - 1). At z=0, factor is 0 (perfect order). At z=39, factor is 1 (maximum chaos). Then: pow(factor, 2.0) to accelerate the onset. Low-Z slices look pristine; high-Z slices look dissolved. The pow exponent is a pedagogical choice: linear would be boring, pow(2) creates a runway.

stages.title: Why the player walks through it
stages.thinking: The grid runs along Z. The player enters from z=0 and walks forward. They begin inside perfect order — rows and columns visible, countable. A few steps forward, the lattice starts to shimmer. Halfway through, it's a haze. At the end, it's noise. You walk from countable space into uncountable space. Entropy is not told, it is traversed.
stages.code:
# Player path: enter at (0, 0, 0), walk toward +z
# 
# z=0:  [▪][▪][▪][▪][▪]  perfect rows
# z=10: [▪][▪][▪][▪][▪]  tiny quivers
# z=20: [▪▪][▪] [▪][▪ ]  lines breaking up
# z=30: [▪  ▪▪  ▪  ]   pattern disintegrating
# z=39: [ ▪ ▪ ▪    ]    pure noise
#
# The Z axis IS a time axis —
# time since order was established.
# Walking Z is walking the arrow of time.

stages.title: Every point knows its entropy
stages.thinking: Each sphere can carry a color that encodes its local entropy — blue for ordered, red for chaotic. That color comes from the same `curved_entropy` that drives the jitter. The player doesn't just see disorder; they see a gradient, a temperature. Color as measurement. (This is why the Color sequence came before randomness — you need to know what paint does before you can paint entropy.)
stages.code:
# Per-point color from local entropy
var point_color = Color(
	curved_entropy,           # red = chaos
	0.3,                       # green constant
	1.0 - curved_entropy       # blue = order
)

# If the point scene exposes set_color:
if point_instance.has_method("set_color"):
	point_instance.set_color(point_color)

# Referenced from color sequence — same paint, new meaning.
# The gradient IS the entropy function made visual.

stages.title: The PRNG is deterministic and that is the point
stages.thinking: randf_range uses Godot's pseudo-random generator. Given the same seed, the exact same 'chaos' appears every time. Call randomize() in _ready() and the seed varies across sessions, so the grid dissolves differently each run. This is a crucial subtlety: what looks random is reproducible. Every PRNG is a clockwork that imitates noise. True randomness (radioactive decay, thermal fluctuation) is not accessible from code.
stages.code:
# Default: deterministic across runs
func _ready() -> void:
	generate_entropy_grid()

# To make each session different:
func _ready() -> void:
	randomize()  # seeds the PRNG from system clock
	generate_entropy_grid()

# To reproduce a specific 'chaos':
func _ready() -> void:
	seed(42)
	generate_entropy_grid()

# Every call to randf_range steps the PRNG state.
# The sequence is fixed once seeded.
# 'Random' here means 'statistically uniform,'
# not 'unpredictable in principle.'

stages.title: Expose the parameters so chaos is tunable
stages.thinking: max_randomness, min_randomness, grid dimensions — all @export. In the editor or via apply_grid_config, the map author can tune the gradient. More randomness: chaos starts earlier. Taller grid: longer runway. Smaller max: dissolution never completes. These aren't just cosmetic; they control the pedagogical experience. Each parameter change tells a different story about how order breaks.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: An entropy axiom knows what it is. Not a field of shaking cubes — a spatial embodiment of the arrow of time. The Z axis is not a direction in 3D; it is the forgetting of a pattern. The player walks from a place where everything has its coordinates to a place where nothing does. The critical parameter is max_randomness because it controls whether the end of the journey looks like annihilation (high) or merely weathering (low). What this artifact cannot hold: the information-theoretic formalization, the reversibility of microstates, the coupling between entropy and free energy. Those arrive at QFEP, where this whole sequence finds its math.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: a 10×10×40 grid where XY offsets grow with Z — perfect order at z=0 dissolves into chaos at z=max via quadratic entropy ramp
# desire: learner walks the Z axis as a time axis and feels pattern dissolving around them
# critical_parameter: max_randomness — how complete the final chaos is; pow(factor, 2.0) controls the onset curve
# triggers: _ready generates the full volume once; no runtime chaos drift — the gradient is static, the WALK is the event
# emerges: the arrow of time as a physical direction; color-coded entropy as a readable field; the difference between pseudo and true randomness
# needs: triple nested grid [has]; color encoding [has]; apply_grid_config [has]; live chaos tuning [missing — fixed at startup]
# relationships: opposite of Tutorial_Single (pure order vs dissolving order); precedes Random_Cubes (single scatter vs gradient); sets up noise sequence (correlated randomness)
# truth: entropy is not disorder — it is the loss of the rule that made order possible
